episode_thesis: Across four papers (Galanter on negative correlation, Quantica on equity/trend/gold/bond mixes, SG's trend indicator paper, Arthur Seep on trend-following systems) Yoav Git argues that an asset's value to a portfolio comes from its correlation and capital efficiency, not its standalone Sharpe: trend is zero-correlated to what it trades by construction, has a Sharpe broadly similar to 60/40, and therefore merits a large share of portfolio risk (near 30%) even though the last year or two were poor. He also argues that replication by correlation is meaningless because almost any CTA is 80-90% correlated with the index, so the real question is a manager's added mean return, and that speed choice matters less than risk scaling and portfolio-level diversification. The host adds the allocator's side: committees want long track records and a diversified set of risk mitigators.

speakers.name: Yoav Git
speakers.role: co-host; systematic trend-following practitioner and researcher (captioned 'Yov', 'Y of Git')
speakers.speaker_note: Recorded around 19 June 2025 (index data as of Wednesday 18 June; US holiday the day before); he was visiting his parents in Israel during the Israel-Iran conflict. Ledger corrections applied: the allocator-justification passage, the list of defensive strategies (option buying, fast trend convexity, trend at the alpha/hedge boundary, quality long-short equity) is his, not the host's; on SG's paper he said the industry has moved slower by checking which speed of the simple indicator correlates with the SG index, not that correlation with slow variants rose over time. Caption: the transcript says 'higher correlation' where lower or negative is meant.

worldview_premises.premise: For a long-term allocation, a strategy with low or negative correlation to the existing portfolio adds risk-adjusted return even with a lower Sharpe, flat or losing, because it lowers overall portfolio volatility; high-volatility negatively correlated strategies are capital efficient, so small allocations hedge meaningfully.
worldview_premises.support: Galanter's allocation formula; two-year example where a high-vol manager with about -30% equity correlation beat a multistrat with 12% correlation and stronger returns.

worldview_premises.premise: In real life the hard part for an allocator is justifying a low-Sharpe diversifier to the investment committee even when the maths shows it adds value; the paper does not address that.
worldview_premises.support: Allocator experience (corrected to him from the ledger).

worldview_premises.premise: Defensive strategies come in several forms (tail-protect option buying, fast trend with higher convexity like buying options paid for with realised rather than implied volatility, trend at the boundary between alpha and hedge, high-quality long-short equity), each with capacity limits (fast trend programs about 1-2 billion, options).
worldview_premises.support: Industry knowledge; quality factor traced to Graham and Barra since the 1970s.

worldview_premises.premise: Catastrophe bonds give return streams uncorrelated with 60/40, whereas private equity and private credit are not clearly diversifying because they stay exposed to the same economic factors as long equity.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from factor exposure; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is zero correlated to the traded assets by construction because long and short are symmetric, unlike a defensive strategy whose negative correlation may not persist; a tail-protect strategy only works if puts are bought continuously.
worldview_premises.support: Construction argument; contrast with option skipping to save money.

worldview_premises.premise: Because trend is symmetric and zero correlated it can be overlaid on any long-only exposure (Bitcoin, gold, equities, bonds) and stays additive.
worldview_premises.support: Symmetry of long and short positions.

worldview_premises.premise: Bonds were negatively correlated with equities in falling-rate, falling-inflation periods, but the correlation is not stable in inflation; 60/40 had a Sharpe of about 0.76 since 1990 and only about 0.55 since 2000, while CTAs have about 0.5 for 2000-2025, similar and uncorrelated.
worldview_premises.support: Quoted Sharpe ratios by period; Quantica numbers.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors judge trend on the last year or two and so miss its structural long-term benefit and zero correlation to 60/40 (recency bias in manager evaluation).
worldview_premises.support: Observation of allocators; no survey.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following works at almost all speeds and in commodities, equities and bonds because people buy winners and sell losers; returns come from capturing return autocorrelation and drift; over the last 25 years nearly all speeds and rule types of the three schools (Turtle breakout, European moving average, time-series momentum) made money.
worldview_premises.support: Seep's scan of speeds and rule types over 25 years; early crisis-alpha demonstration in 2008.

worldview_premises.premise: Transparency (the 2011-12 time-series momentum paper, preceded by managers keeping methods secret because a simple rule looks trivial) made trend commonplace and harder to charge for, so many investors are reluctant to pay for it despite its alpha.
worldview_premises.support: Personal experience at Winton and AHL (anecdote of Anthony Daniels).

worldview_premises.premise: Almost any CTA is 80-90% correlated with the CTA index, so correlation to a benchmark is not informative for replication and ignores the mean; the relevant question for a manager is the added mean return over a highly correlated, zero-alpha index.
worldview_premises.support: SG's simple trend indicator is about 80% correlated with the SG CTA index yet returned only 0.43% a year with 16% volatility (Sharpe about 0.03, the host's reading) since 2002; the SG CTA Index has a Sharpe about 0.4 out of sample after costs.

worldview_premises.premise: A CTA adds value by raising Sharpe slightly in each market through execution, nonlinear filters, fast/slow switching, cost reduction and risk management.
worldview_premises.support: His working life; no measured decomposition.

worldview_premises.premise: The CTA industry has become slower, and trend constituents decorrelate from the simple SG indicator in high-vol crises (April 2025, Covid, Taper Tantrum) but converge back quickly.
worldview_premises.support: SG indicator correlations at different speeds, and Commitments of Traders positioning versus trend indicators.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility estimation and risk scaling was the major innovation in trend following; a 12-month TSMOM equal-weights returns and is optimal for capturing drift unless one has a strong view that autocorrelation varies through the year.
worldview_premises.support: Seep's derivation of optimal speed for white noise, AR(1) and fractional ARMA processes.

worldview_premises.premise: 12-month TSMOM has little positive skew (slightly negative) while its alpha is good.
worldview_premises.support: Backtest in Seep's paper as he describes it.

decision_process.practice: Put close to 30% of portfolio risk in trend alongside 60/40, based on uncorrelated forward Sharpe of 0.7 versus 0.3.
decision_process.why: Zero correlation makes it additive even at a lower Sharpe.

decision_process.practice: A beginner can stop at 12-month TSMOM on volatility-adjusted returns; tilt between fast and slow only for portfolio diversification.
decision_process.why: TSMOM is near optimal at capturing drift; tilting adds value only when autocorrelation view is strong or a signal hedges the book.

decision_process.practice: Give more risk to signals or markets that currently hedge the rest of the trend book (negative correlation); many CTAs do not.
Test strategies with negative-lag look-ahead and random-noise runs, and benchmark to simulated known processes.
Evaluate a CTA by added mean return over a high-correlation index, not by correlation.
Estimate volatility and risk-scale positions properly.
decision_process.why: The major innovation in trend following.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The host says he and Yoav only saw the Quantica quarterly report an hour or two earlier and have not read it in detail, so all Quantica Sharpe figures are second-hand and from a skim.
Quantica's trend result for the 1990s uses a proxy because the SG Trend Index does not exist before 2000, so the full-period trend Sharpe depends on a constructed series.
The paper's quoted 'higher correlation' is probably a slip for lower or negative correlation.
The 'almost 30% of risk in trend' figure uses a simple two-asset logic with assumed forward Sharpes of 0.7 and 0.3 and ignores costs, leverage limits and capacity.

SG's simple indicator is shown with a Sharpe of about 0.03 (host) while the CTA index is about 0.4 (Yoav); the comparison mixes cost-free indicator and after-cost index and does not state that the indicator figure is gross.
Statement that trend works at almost all speeds over 25 years is from Seep's paper, said to have been read in an early draft; no figures are given.
Private equity and private credit are called not diversifying on factor-exposure reasoning; no evidence beyond that.
Whether a speed tilt works out of sample is left unanswered when the host asks; the answer shifts to portfolio diversification.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Yoav treats forward Sharpe assumptions for 60/40 (about 0.7) and CTA (about 0.3), and the correlation between them (near zero), as the inputs that fix trend's share of risk; the stability of the stock-bond correlation (falling versus rising inflation) as the input that decides whether bonds keep diversifying; and cross-market signal correlation inside the trend book as the input for speed tilts. The host watches the trend barometer (48, neutral), sector contributions (oil reversing, financials hurting) and short-term versus trend indices. Horizon is multi-year for allocation and weeks for the trend book.
reader_inferences: (reader) Yoav's argument is a portfolio-variance one: size follows correlation and capital efficiency, so a strategy with Sharpe near half of 60/40's can still deserve a third of risk; this contradicts the common screening by standalone Sharpe.

(reader) His replication point implies that high correlation to a trend index is a weak test of manager quality, and the useful test is net-of-cost added Sharpe relative to a transparent trend benchmark.
(reader) The two speakers diverge in emphasis: Yoav on mathematical structure (zero correlation by construction, optimal speed), Niels on empirical track records and allocator practicalities.

(reader) Both agree that the poor 2025 YTD CTA returns are not evidence against the long-run case; both warn against extrapolating the past one or two years in either direction (bonds in 1990-2021, trend in 2024-25).
